hero.intro: I work on applied deep learning, most recently on detecting disease in corn leaves from images. My focus is on models that can be evaluated honestly — documented data, reproducible splits, and results reported as they are.

about.title: Research first, engineering close behind
about.description: The short version of why the work looks like this — and what I would rather not pretend.
paragraphs: I'm an AI researcher and builder based in {location}. My work sits at the intersection of applied deep learning and the practical question of whether a model does anything useful outside a notebook.

My undergraduate thesis compared DenseNet121 and EfficientNet-B0 for detecting disease in corn leaves from images. It was my first sustained piece of research, and the most valuable part wasn't the modelling — it was learning how much of a result depends on decisions made before training starts: how the data is split, what is held out, and what the number on the screen actually describes.

I studied software engineering at Daffodil International University, graduating in June 2026. That background shapes how I approach research: I'd rather ship something reproducible than something impressive — and I can build the surrounding system, not just the experiment.

I'm at the beginning of a research career and I'd rather say that plainly than inflate it. What I have is work I can explain end to end, and a clear direction: computer vision applied to problems where the data is messy and the stakes are real.

principles.title: Report what the model actually did
principles.body: A number is only useful if someone can re-run it. Datasets, splits and seeds get documented alongside the result, not after it.

principles.title: Prefer the boring baseline
principles.body: New architectures are easy to justify after the fact. I try to establish what a simpler model achieves first, then argue for complexity with evidence.

principles.title: Build the thing, not just the notebook
principles.body: A trained model that nobody can run is a claim, not a system. I care about the path from experiment to something usable.
